text.hook:
std::unique_ptr is the default owning pointer.
Interviewers use it to test ownership, deleters and moved-from state.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. One owner plus a cleanup policy
2. What a move really transfers
3. get, release, reset
4. Custom deleters and their size
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Ownership transfer, deleters and arrays: what interviewers actually check.

slides.title: Exclusive ownership plus a cleanup policy

cards.label: `T* ptr`
cards.text: Points to the managed object, usually on the heap.

slides.takeaway: Copy is deleted, ownership only moves. With the default deleter it is one pointer, same code as a raw pointer.

slides.title: `auto p2 = std::move(p1);` step by step
steps: `std::move` is only a cast. It moves nothing.
the move constructor copies the stored pointer into `p2`
`p1` is set to `nullptr`: guaranteed empty, not "unspecified"
the object never moved: same address, no allocation

slides.title: `get`, `release`, `reset`
rows: **given up**: returns the pointer, frees nothing
stores `q` **first**, then deletes the old object
slides.takeaway: The deleter is never called on null: no `fclose(nullptr)` through a `unique_ptr`.

slides.title: The deleter is part of the type (libstdc++, x86-64)
slides.takeaway: Different deleters, different types: they cannot share one `std::vector`. (`shared_ptr` type-erases the deleter.)

slides.title: Scalar vs array form

cards.label: `make_unique<T[]>(n)`
cards.text: Calls `delete[]`: n destructors, in reverse index order.

slides.takeaway: It does not know its size. Prefer `std::vector`, keep `unique_ptr<T[]>` for fixed buffers handed to C APIs.

slides.title: The destructor goes in the .cpp
slides.takeaway: An implicit destructor deletes `Impl` where it is incomplete: "invalid application of 'sizeof' to incomplete type".

items.truth: Only the stored pointer is transferred. The object stays at the same address.
For `unique_ptr` it is guaranteed empty. `p1->f()` is a null dereference: UB.
`make_unique` or `new` constructs it. `unique_ptr` owns and destroys it.

items.myth: "A custom deleter always increases the size."
items.truth: Stateless deleters add nothing. Function pointers and state do.

items.myth: "`reset(q)` deletes the old object, then stores `q`."
items.truth: It stores `q` first, then deletes the old object.

items.myth: "In C++17 you still need `make_unique` for exception safety."
items.truth: That argument-interleaving leak is gone in C++17. Prefer it anyway: no naked `new`.

slides.hero:
One owner.
Moves, never copies.

`reset()` frees.
`release()` lets go.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The author wanted to free a 1 MiB buffer early.
One call on a unique_ptr. Did it work?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The compiler stays silent, even with -Wall -Wextra.

slides.title:
"Done with it."
What happens to the buffer?

slides.verdict: A. `buf` is null, and the buffer leaks
slides.verdict_sub: LeakSanitizer: the vector and its 1 MiB buffer. GCC 11: no warning
bullets: `release()` only gives up ownership: it nulls the stored pointer and **returns** the old one.
The returned pointer is discarded here. Nothing is deleted.
libstdc++ 11 does not mark `release()` `[[nodiscard]]`, so `-Wall -Wextra` are silent.
`release()` hands responsibility to the caller. `reset()` is the one that frees.

slides.title: Map the intent to the right call
slides.code:
buf.reset();             // free it now
buf = nullptr;           // same thing

q = std::move(buf);      // hand to q
api_adopt(buf.release()); // C API owns it
slides.takeaway: `release()` without using its result is always a leak.

text.hook:
A lambda captures a unique_ptr by move.
Then it goes into a std::function.
Does this compile?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: A pattern that shows up in every task queue and callback API.

slides.title:
Does this compile?
If yes, what does it print?

bullets: The init-capture is fine: the closure owns the `unique_ptr`, so it is **move-only**.
`std::function` requires a copy-constructible target, even if you never copy it.
Moving the lambda in does not help.
slides.wrong: "A: 10, then 10, the lambda was moved in"

slides.title: `std::move_only_function`
bullets: Or keep the closure as `auto` / a template parameter.
Or capture a `std::shared_ptr` if it must be copyable.
slides.takeaway: Owning a `unique_ptr` makes the enclosing type move-only, lambdas included.

text.hook:
unique_ptr<Base> holding a Derived.
No warning at -Wall, no crash in tests.
Ship it?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The bug hides well: switch the same code to shared_ptr and it seems to work.

slides.title: Is this correct?

bullets: The converting move turns the deleter into `default_delete<Base>`: `delete (Base*)p`.
Without a virtual destructor that is UB. In practice `~Derived` never runs.
ASan: new-delete-type-mismatch. With that check off, LSan reports `big`'s 65-byte buffer.
GCC `-Wall` is silent: `Base` has no other virtual functions.

slides.title: Two correct designs
slides.tip: `shared_ptr` captures the deleter at creation and calls `~Derived`. That hides the bug.

text.hook:
A function only reads an Order.
The caller owns it through a unique_ptr.
"Pass the smart pointer by const&." Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Your signature documents ownership. Reviewers read it that way.

slides.title: Which parameter type for `print`?
slides.cta: Pick A, B, C or D, then swipe ➜

slides.verdict_sub: Ownership is not involved, so the signature should not mention it
bullets: `const unique_ptr&` ties `print` to one owner type. `s` and `local` cannot call it.
`unique_ptr` by value is a **sink**: `print` would take and destroy the order.
`unique_ptr&&`: a sink that may not move. The caller cannot be sure it is empty.

slides.title: Signatures document ownership
slides.code:
void use(const Order& o);         // use
void sink(std::unique_ptr<Order> p); // sink
void reseat(std::unique_ptr<Order>& p);
std::unique_ptr<Order> make();     // factory
slides.tip: Sink: caller writes `sink(std::move(u))`, `u` is null after. Factory: `return p;` with no `std::move`.
slides.takeaway: Core Guidelines: R.32 by value to sink, R.33 `&` to reseat, F.7 `T*` or `T&` when ownership is not involved.
